En estos años, de los restos encontrados solo se comprobaron cuatro restos\nóseos aislados, que pertenecen a tres jóvenes de Ayotzinapa, Alexander\nMora Venancio, Christian Rodríguez Telumbre y Jhosivany Guerrero\nde la Cruz. El primero de ellos se encontró en una diligencia falsa de 2014\nen el río San Juan, al parecer en una bolsa. Tenía grandes diferencias con los\notros restos óseos carbonizados o cremados que se hallaban en dicha bolsa. Era\nligeramente más grande en tamaño y estaba menos afectado por exposición a\naltas temperaturas, lo que podría indicar que la fuente de donde proviene podría\nno ser la misma, como señaló en su momento el EAAF. Los otros tres restos\nóseos que correspondientes a los otros dos estudiantes, fueron encontrados en la\n15\n\nUna visión global sobre los hechos, las responsabilidades y la situación del caso Ayotzinapa\nBarranca de la Carnicería, con la actuación profesional y trasparente llevada a\ncabo por la UEILCA, 5-6 años después de los hechos (2019-2020). Tampoco se\nencontraron otros restos óseos identificables de los mismos muchachos, es decir\notras partes de sus cuerpos.\nEste descubrimiento podría ser compatible con la versión de un testigo protegido\nque señaló que partes de los cuerpos de los normalistas asesinados habrían sido\nllevados a dos funerarias, donde una parte habría sido cremada no totalmente o\ncarbonizada y otros cuerpos no se llegaron a incinerar por la cantidad e imposibilidad\nde llevarlo a cabo en ese tiempo. Señaló también que los restos de los muchachos se\nhabrían repartido entre diferentes células de GU con distintos destinos para ocultar\nlo sucedido, incluyendo un rancho donde se llevaban a cabo anteriormente acciones\npara disolver cuerpos en ácido. Sin embargo, hay información documental recogida\npor SEDENA que refiere al menos un grupo de muchachos se encontrarían vivos\nvarios días después del 26 de septiembre de 2014.\nLa UEILCA ha seguido trabajando en procesos de búsqueda. Estamos a la\nespera de los resultados de los nuevos hallazgos.\n27. Muchos testigos y participantes en los hechos miembros de GU han sido\nasesinados en estos años, algunos de ellos intencionalmente para impedir\nla investigación. Eso hace que la posibilidad de contar con información\nsignificativa sobre el destino de los jóvenes haya sido cada vez menor, a pesar\nde los avances que han sido relevantes y en medio de algunas acciones de\nobstrucción. El último hecho grave conllevó el asesinato de un presunto alto\nresponsable y testigo de los hechos, conocido como El Caderas, muerto en\nun operativo policial de 23 impactos de bala cuando iba a ser detenido, que\nmuestra una acción intencional de eliminarlo, cuando era alguien que podría\nproporcionar mucha información. La participación en dicho operativo de todos\nlos que intervinieron y de policías que no estaban encargados de esa acción\ny sin embargo participaron, es un hecho de extrema gravedad, que tiene que\nser investigado porque, además de la posible ejecución extrajudicial, muestra\nun intento de seguir coartando la investigación y el derecho a la verdad de\nlos familiares. Hasta ahora, no se ha conocido ningún paso significativo en la\ninvestigación de este hecho.\n28. Ningún avance se ha dado en estos años sobre la investigación del tráfico de\nheroína, armas y/o dinero y caso del 5° autobús tomado por los estudiantes.\nDicho bus fue el único no atacado esa noche, salió escoltado por la Policía\nFederal hacia la caseta 3 en la salida de Iguala, su recorrido fue confirmado\npor el GPS, se confirmó la versión de los jóvenes sobre su existencia y sobre\nsu recorrido inicial en Iguala, dicho bus estuvo parado antes del Palacio de\n16\n\nA ocho años y medio del caso\nJusticia, fue visto por testigos civiles y también por personal militar que ocultó\nese hecho durante 7 años. La persona entrevistada como chofer de ese 5° bus\nmintió en su declaración ante la PGR, institución que no quiso investigar este\nhecho en 2015-2016.\nEl GIEI recibió de la PGR respuestas negativas sobre la existencia de\ninvestigaciones sobre tráfico de heroína y dinero a través de buses de pasajeros.\nSin embargo, unos meses antes de los hechos, la propia PGR y el ejército habían\nparticipado en un operativo de detención e incautación de un bus modificado para\nel transporte de heroína y dinero a EE. UU. Este hecho y sus responsabilidades\nsigue sin ser investigados, cuando contribuirían a esclarecer no solo parte de los\nhechos en este caso, sino de las rutas y modalidades del transporte de drogas\nilegales en Iguala y México hacia EE. UU.\n29. Muchas personas miembros de diferentes organismos deben ser todavía\nllamados a declarar. Entre ellos cargos y agentes del CISEN, miembros del\ngobierno de Guerrero, PGJ, Fiscales y MP, policías estatales y ministeriales,\nademás de ex miembros de SEIDO, autoridades militares y de Policía Federal,\nautoridades de gobernación, entre otros. Estas declaraciones señalamos que\ndeberán ser contrastadas con los datos objetivos y lo que se conoce en el\nconjunto de la investigación, para evitar volver a diligencias poco sustantivas\no repetitivas como ha sucedido. Algunas de estas personas clave han huido\ndel país al ser investigadas, habiendo casos de complicidad de quienes siendo\nresponsables no llevaron a cabo las detenciones o proporcionaron protección o\ninformación para su huida, incluyendo contactos al parecer en la propia FGR.\nEstas acciones deben ser también investigadas por obstrucción a la justicia.\n30. El uso de nuevos testigos y contraste de información. Respecto al uso de\ndiferentes testigos y testigos protegidos el GIEI ha alertado a la Fiscalía de que\nse necesita evaluar la consistencia y el contraste con otras fuentes y pruebas\npara tener mayor confianza en las informaciones, incluyendo su utilización en\nlas diligencias de búsqueda que se están llevando a cabo.\n31. La actuación del despacho del Fiscal General y de la División de Asuntos\nInternos en la UEILCA en agosto de 2022 y las presiones llevadas a cabo\ncontra el fiscal del caso y su equipo, llevaron a la salida del Fiscal Omar\nGómez Trejo y gran parte de su equipo de la UEILCA. La intervención de\nAsuntos Internos, a pesar de ser presentada como una revisión rutinaria, tuvo\ndos objetivos invadiendo la competencia de la UEILCA. Por una parte, revocar\n21 órdenes de captura sobre sujetos del ejército, juez de barandillas y otros,\nque habían sido concedidas por un juez que había encontrado sin embargo\nsuficientes elementos para ello; y por otra parte, presionar a los funcionarios de\n17\n\nUna visión global sobre los hechos, las responsabilidades y la situación del caso Ayotzinapa\nla UEILCA para presentar de forma acelerada acusaciones por investigaciones\nque estaban en curso.\nLa actuación de Asuntos Internos supone un obstáculo a la independencia\nde la Fiscalía especial, hecho que fue denunciado por el GIEI en el mismo\nmomento que sucedió en 2022, y que no ha sido investigado. Se debe evitar\nque funcionarios que tuvieron una actuación cuestionable en la investigación en\n2016-2018 de funcionarios de la PGR autores de la construcción de la llamada\nVerdad Histórica, sigan teniendo poder dentro de la Fiscalía como sucede\nactualmente. Sin la necesaria independencia, imparcialidad y conocimiento del\ncaso, la fiscalía ve y verá limitado su trabajo.\nLa fiscalía corre el riesgo de que se difieran las investigaciones y capturas, y\nno se llegue a esclarecer el caso a pesar de contar con la información que ya se\nencuentra disponible y que se retarden o se limiten las acciones de investigación\nque aún hay que llevar adelante. Por otra parte, la realización de diligencias\nde investigación, toma de nuevas declaraciones y otras pruebas, debe hacerse\nutilizando toda la experiencia previa y preparando dichas diligencias con todas\nlas herramientas y conocimiento existente para tener los necesarios elementos\nde contraste que hagan realmente avanzar la investigación.\n32. El informe de la COVAJ. Hay que reiterar que el informe de la COVAJ\npresentado en agosto de 2022 no tiene que ver con la judicialización, dado que\nse trata de una instancia extrajudicial, y sus revelaciones respecto a los hechos\nse basan (parcialmente) en la evidencia del GIEI y la UEILCA, además de la\nsuya propia. La determinación por parte de dicha comisión de que se trata de un\nCrimen de Estado está basada en las pruebas existentes.\nSin embargo, como ya se señaló, otra parte de dicho informe recogía capturas\nde pantalla de mensajes de whatsApp. Para el GIEI los mensajes analizados\nno pueden considerarse como una prueba digital y no es posible garantizar la\noriginalidad de las capturas de pantalla que se presentaron como prueba en\ndicho informe, dada la inconsistencia de los metadatos y otros aspectos clave\nde los mensajes que demostró un peritaje encargado por el GIEI a un experto en\n“informática forense” y que ha sido entregado a la Fiscalía, a la COVAJ y a los\nrepresentantes. Como se señaló en octubre de 2022, las características de esos\nmensajes contrastan enormemente con las de los mensajes PIN de las escuchas\ntelefónicas y mensajes de Chicago, que muestran el tipo de comunicaciones que\ntenían efectivamente los miembros del grupo criminal.\nCinco meses después de ser entregados por la COVAJ a la Fiscalía los teléfonos\ndonde supuestamente se habrían registrado dichos mensajes, no se ha realizado\n18\n\nA ocho años y medio del caso\nun análisis de los mismos que sigue estando pendiente. Advertimos de que la\nforma en que llegaron a esa investigación debe ser objeto de verificación para\ngenerar las condiciones de validez como prueba.\nHemos tratado de ayudar a reconstruir la confianza para bien de la credibilidad\nde las instituciones y el derecho de las víctimas a la verdad y la justicia, así como\ndisminuir el impacto que las revelaciones del contenido no contrastadas tuvieron\nen las víctimas. Hemos insistido al gobierno y la fiscalía en la importancia\nde prevenir en el futuro que se haga pública cualquier acción no contrastada\npreviamente, ni informada a los padres y madres y sus representantes, y\ncontrastada con el GIEI que fue precisamente creado para coadyuvar en la\ninvestigación, y debe seguir los estándares de investigación en estos casos.\n33. Respecto a las investigaciones y judicializaciones, la renovación de más del\n95% de la unidad especial del caso Ayotzinapa, tras las dimisiones y cambios\nrealizados a partir de septiembre de 2022 en la UEILCA, ha generado, como\nya alertó el GIEI en su momento, retrasos considerables en tres cuestiones que\nresultan fundamentales para la investigación:\n1. Pérdida de la información contextual, del expediente y de conocimiento del\ncaso por parte de quienes tienen que llevar la investigación adelante en la\nactualidad. Hay que tener en cuenta que se está en fase de llevar a cabo\ncapturas, procesos de judicialización y en otros casos de llegar a sentencias,\nen donde el conocimiento del caso y la experiencia y compromiso de los\nfiscales es determinante.\n2. Pérdida de confianza y aproximación a testigos colaboradores que habían\ntenido un papel clave en el esclarecimiento de aspectos fundamentales del\ncaso y la búsqueda de los desaparecidos. Sin la colaboración y protección de\nestos testigos, hay parte de la investigación que no podría seguir adelante,\nasí como se limita el acercamiento de otros posibles testigos que necesitan\nprotección para poder colaborar.\n3. Retrasos en la consistencia de consignaciones e imputaciones por causa de la\nfragmentación de la información.\n34. El cumplimiento de las judicializaciones y órdenes de aprehensión que se\nretiraron después de haber sido concedidas por el juez y mediante un fiscal\nque no pertenecía a la UEILCA y así como de otras pendientes, tiene que\ntener un nuevo impulso que ayude a poner toda la energía en la resolución\ndel caso. Actualmente solo una parte de las detenciones que cuentan ya con\nórdenes de aprensión se han materializado. Tanto en países como Israel o EE.\nUU. se encuentran responsables de la tortura y cuya actuación supuso una\n19\n\nUna visión global sobre los hechos, las responsabilidades y la situación del caso Ayotzinapa\ncolaboración con la desaparición por el desvío de la investigación. Respecto\nal personal militar, respecto al cual hay cuatro detenidos, el GIEI ha señalado\nespecialmente las consideradas prioritarias.\nRevisada en su integridad la carga laboral de la UEILCA, es claro que sólo se están\nimpulsando algunos de todos los procesos que se venían adelantando. Hay que\nrecordar que la investigación del caso se basa en tres factores cuyo seguimiento es\ndeterminante para que la investigación no pierda coherencia e impulso:\n1. La obstrucción, la falsificación de documentos oficiales, las omisiones\ndolosas de información relevante, y las respuestas negando información\nque si existe en la investigación y construcción de la llamada verdad\nhistórica, que desvió la búsqueda de los jóvenes y las responsabilidades de\nlos hechos.\n2. La tortura con la cual se llevaron a cabo las autoinculpaciones en este caso, que\nfinalmente se cayeron en el paso ante los jueces y que pervirtió la veracidad\nde posibles hallazgos y limitó las responsabilidades. La investigación de los\nejecutores y de quienes conocieron, supieron o debían saber sobre dichas\nprácticas.\n3. La responsabilidad por los hechos del 26 y 27 de septiembre de 2014, en\ntérminos de la detención, homicidio, tentativas de homicidio y desaparición,\ncomo de las acciones que las hicieron posible por la parálisis y falta de\nprotección de instituciones del Estado mexicano.\nLa información que se nos ha proporcionado de varias de esas averiguaciones o\ncarpetas que venían adelantándose, muestra que no se mueven desde hace algún\ntiempo dadas las condiciones señaladas.\nAsí mismo, se necesita adelantar nuevas investigaciones por la obstrucción,\nfalsedad u omisión de información. Esto sucede por ejemplo en comunicaciones\nde Sedena y Marina en que niegan la existencia de informaciones que han\nsido ya conocidas documentalmente por el GIEI, y que sin embargo no se ha\nproporcionado a la UEILCA. También en las declaraciones de miembros de\nesas y otras instituciones se ha ocultado información y faltado a la verdad, lo\nque debe llevar a que se investiguen estos hechos.\nSegún nos han informado, en principio se están impulsando de manera prioritaria\ndos de las investigaciones, la que pertenecía a las 83 consignaciones y la que se\nadelanta contra el exprocurador de la PGR, Murillo Karam.\n20\n\nA ocho años y medio del caso\nEstas averiguaciones y/o carpetas, algunas de ellas con imputado conocido,\notras abiertas contra quien resulte responsable, son fundamentales para poder\ndeterminar responsabilidades, tanto sobre los hechos como de todas las formas\nde obstrucción, que en últimas se constituyen en formas de perpetuar la\ndesaparición forzada con participación de todos los actores institucionales que\npermitieron mantener el ocultamiento modificando las versiones, los hechos y\nlas actas. Estas acciones, como parte de un acto sistemático, han implicado la\npérdida de información vital para el hallazgo de los estudiantes desde el día 1\nde las agresiones.\n34. F ortalecer la justicia, integrar responsabilidades y evitar la fragmentación.\nLa necesidad de actuar en consecuencia contra todos los que de una u otra manera\nalteraron y cometieron los hechos es fundamental y ha sido el compromiso\nadquirido públicamente por las más altas autoridades del Estado, para lograr\nimpartir justicia, conocer la verdad.\nEste caso muestra la cooptación de responsables institucionales civiles y militares\ny de seguridad que permiten entender no sólo su actuación sino la cooptación\npor la delincuencia organizada de parte de las autoridades estatales, federales y\nmunicipales de todo orden, que estuvieron involucradas en los hechos. Algunas\nde estas condiciones siguen dándose en la actualidad en Iguala. La no impunidad\nen este caso es una oportunidad para México de tener una transformación efectiva\nen el tema de la justicia y el respeto a los derechos humanos.\nLas más de 33 causas, que ya se encuentran en juicio en los juzgados Octavo\nde Morelos, Noveno de Guerrero, Primero de Tamaulipas, Tercero del Estado\nde México, Quinto de Iguala, así como en Tribunales Superiores, permiten\nobservar que la labor de investigación y de juzgamiento exige una perfecta\ncoordinación entre todos los casos pues responden a un contexto común que\ndebe estar actualizado a la realidad de lo que se ha encontrado. Los elementos\nprobatorios que se producen en cualquiera de estas investigaciones y en los\njuicios deben ser objeto de conocimiento y control por todos los fiscales que\npuedan utilizar estos elementos para sus investigaciones, causas o procesos.\nPor esa razón, el GIEI desde su primer comunicado en 2015, hasta el conjunto\nde sus actuaciones e informes, ha señalado reiteradamente que al ser un hecho\ncomplejo y entendiéndose como macro caso, debe manejarse en forma conexa\npara no dejar de incorporar ningún elemento que haga fundamental entender\ncómo fue el modus operandi, pero sobre todo quiénes son los partícipes y que\npor lo menos mantiene a más de 75 detenidos, además de que en este proceso\npueda llegarse a una mayor verdad de lo sucedido y del destino de los jóvenes\ndesaparecidos que es el objetivo último de nuestro trabajo.\n21\n\nUna visión global sobre los hechos, las responsabilidades y la situación del caso Ayotzinapa\n35. Existen otras víctimas cuyos derechos deben ser reconocidos, los casos\ninvestigados y la reparación hecha efectiva. Al menos 31 personas resultaron\nheridas y lesionadas en los diferentes ataques, con distintos grados de afectación\ny/o discapacidad. Uno de los estudiantes está en coma desde los hechos. Hay 6\npersonas que fueron asesinadas, tres de ellas estudiantes. Estos hechos deben ser\nigualmente investigados e incorporados en las distintas carpetas para incluir a\nestas víctimas y tener mayores elementos de prueba que eviten la fragmentación\nde la investigación.\n36. La situación de familiares y víctimas. Los familiares han mantenido en\nestos últimos años su esperanza de una resolución efectiva, pero también han\nexpresado su frustración por los obstáculos encontrados en la investigación\ny que necesitan ser removidos. Al impacto acumulado de los hechos,\nla pérdida de sus hijos y los intentos de limitar el avance del caso, se han\nsumado intentos de desestructurar sus procesos organizativos con presiones\npolíticas y económicas en Guerrero. El GIEI ha alertado a las autoridades\nde algunas maniobras de las que ha tenido conocimiento y que señalan a\npersonajes del estado de Guerrero en intentos de manipulación. También se\nhan dado señalamientos contra abogados representantes de las víctimas, de\norganizaciones como Tlachinollan o el Prodh que se encontraron en archivos\nmilitares que se basan en prejuicios o señalamientos similares a los que ha sido\nobjeto el GIEI en el pasado y que son inaceptables, y de los que se encontró\nrastro en dichos archivos.\nEs importante que se proteja la confianza y el proceso de las víctimas con\nla información transparente y un marco de atención a los familiares en sus\nnecesidades que debe ser claro y fundamentado en los derechos de las víctimas,\ny no en gestiones particulares o selectivas. La construcción de un programa\nde atención sigue siendo, ocho años después de los hechos, una asignatura\npendiente que debe llevarse a cabo con la participación de los familiares y sus\nrepresentantes, para lo que el GIEI ha ofrecido su colaboración. En ningún caso\nesto supone dejar de lado la lucha por la verdad y la justicia, en las que este\ninforme está haciendo énfasis en la situación actual.\nHay que reconocer los avances significativos en la investigación llevados a\ncabo por el Fiscal Omar Gómez y su equipo, que logró avanzar en un número\nmuy amplio las investigaciones hasta donde se encuentran hoy, y que se vieron\npresionados para tener que dimitir en un intento de controlar su independencia\ny de controlar la investigación, debiéndose garantizar su protección.\nComo en el poema de Machado, “Hoy es todavía”, y es esta rendija hacia el\nfuturo es el lugar en el que el GIEI sigue trabajando.\n22", "excerpt_sha256": "a1784b00156291adf1ddd00e74a6940ff18baec7a560d9bc5117372f9691074b", "verification_status": "corrected", Transformation Index", "raw_sha256": "4298ec648952a6ec86129750e787a3505e147eb6ab93d70052afbd3398ab393d", "fact_summary": "BTI reports that the AMLO government created commissions concerning historical "3B.4", "4B.4", "7B.1", "7B.2", "7B.6", "7B.7", "8B.8", "8B.9"], "polarity": "adverse", "period_fit": "The report assesses AMLO's administration and continuing disappearance-investigation policy, with fully specified in the supplied unit."], "start_unit": 11, "end_unit": 11, "locator": "extracted HTML block 11", "exact_excerpt": "Under the AMLO administration, the government created an independent commission to investigate disappearances and crimes committed by the state from 1965 to 1990. It also formed a commission within the Ministry of the Interior to investigate the disappearance of the 43 students from Ayotzinapa. Nevertheless, the AMLO government at some point blocked both initiatives when these commissions sought information about the army. This information would have implicated the military, which is closely linked to the government. A similar situation occurred with the Commission on Human Rights (CNDH), which proved ineffectual under the AMLO government. Although the parliamentary group tasked with selecting the head of the CNDH strongly criticized the official who had led it during the previous administration, it ultimately retained this incumbent to ensure the army would remain unbothered. For the same reasons, the AMLO government refused to meet with one of the prominent leaders of the movement of victims of the war on drugs, poet Javier Sicilia of the Movement for Peace, Justice and Dignity (MPJD). It also proved ineffective in investigating the more than 100,000 people who have been reported missing due to the war on drugs, and it cut resources for victims’ organizations as they criticized the government’s ineffectiveness. In fact, it ultimately changed the methodology used to count the number of disappeared to lower the official number. In protest of the methodological alteration, Karla Quintana, who was in charge of the institution dealing with disappearances, resigned from her post. The government’s reluctance and actions have thus strongly undermined any attempt to advance reconciliation efforts.\nReconciliation\nInternational Cooperation\nAMLO’s government focused primarily on Mexico’s domestic affairs and generally viewed international cooperation as unnecessary (and in some cases, as with external support for critical NGOs, strictly rejected it). A significant exception was Mexico’s relations with the United States. Mexico is highly dependent on its relationship with the United States under the free trade agreement. The strategic partnership between Mexico and the United States aims to secure the U.S.-Mexico border, promote economic growth and create more business opportunities. The Mexican government has sought to navigate a difficult relationship with the White House to avoid disrupting Mexico’s development goals. AMLO and President Sheinbaum have sought to promote regional development (in Mexico and Central America), with an eye toward addressing public safety and immigration by partnering with the United States to channel foreign aid. While the strategy has been clear, the Biden administration was not particularly receptive, and now the second Donald Trump administration is outright hostile toward this approach.\nEffective use of support\nMexico’s primary partnership is with the United States and centers on economic, security and migration issues. Mexico has been largely reliable, though some issues have disrupted this relationship, especially the policies the previous government implemented toward the illegal economy and drug cartels. Regarding economic challenges, there was a significant shift in the government’s energy policy, severely limiting private investment in a sector that had previously been privatized. The government also declared a moratorium on imports of transgenic maize. Both issues have been considered breaches of the free trade agreement, as has the U.S. unilateral adoption of tariffs on Mexican imports.\nRegarding other countries and international organizations, Mexico is widely regarded as a reliable international partner. However, there have been issues affecting Mexico’s reliability, especially with regard to the issue of human rights. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights has condemned Mexico for violating the American Convention on Human Rights in its application of pretrial detention, for its practice of preventive detention to hold migrants, and for the army’s intervention in internal security. The United Nations has also questioned the lack of proper consultations with Indigenous communities in the construction of large infrastructure projects. The International Labour Organization (ILO) has criticized Mexico for violating trade union freedom and for inadequate consultations with social partners in implementing labor reform.\nConsistent with Mexico’s Estrada Doctrine of nonintervention in other countries’ internal affairs, the López Obrador government has adopted an ambiguous posture regarding international events. While some sectors would prefer that top policymakers denounce breaches of human rights; electoral fraud; and the imprisonment of opponents in countries such as Cuba, Venezuela or Nicaragua, the government has made a point of maintaining working relations with all countries. The country has ratified the Paris International Climate Agreement and remains a party to it. Nonetheless, Mexico’s updated Nationally Determined Contributions have increased its overall emissions level.\nCredibility\nMexico’s main regional integration agreement is with the United States and Canada. AMLO’s government showed considerable willingness to work with these two North American partners on several issues. In particular, the government renegotiated the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) to accommodate a hostile Trump administration seeking more favorable terms. With respect to Latin America, the AMLO administration advocated on behalf of Central American countries for the United States to invest in regional development in order to address the high levels of violence and resulting undocumented immigration. Although this advocacy has met with indifference (during the Biden administration) and hostility (during the Trump administration), it reflects Mexico’s cooperation with international partners.\nMexico has also cooperated with the United States on the issues of migration and drug-trafficking. Both areas have become crucial in recent years, especially since the first Trump presidency and the formation of migrant caravans from Central American countries seeking to reach the United States. At the beginning of the first Trump presidency and AMLO’s presidency, Mexico was pressured – through threats to impose tariffs on products from Mexico – to ramp up control of its borders. As a result, AMLO reversed his initial announcement that he would allow migrants to pass through Mexico. Similarly, on the issue of drug-trafficking, the Mexican government cooperated actively with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) to enable the agency to carry out activities in Mexican territory. Both issues continue to be crucial.\nPresident Sheinbaum is pursuing the AMLO administration’s strategy of stopping migrants within Mexico’s borders and of accepting migrants that have been deported from the United States when they are Mexican nationals and, in some instances, when they hold other nationalities. In the area of drug policy, the Trump administration has threatened to act unilaterally if Mexico does not adopt a much more aggressive approach to drug-trafficking; in response, the Sheinbaum government has changed its policy, especially on fentanyl. It has resumed direct anti-drug operations, seizures and arrests of cartel members, activities that had nearly stopped under the previous administration.\nRegional cooperation\nStrategic Outlook\nMexico faces a number of complex challenges relating to security, economic growth, governance and social development. Drug cartels and organized crime groups continue to exert significant influence within the country, leading to high homicide rates, corruption and weakened state institutions. Corruption remains pervasive at the federal, state and municipal levels, undermining governance and economic growth. Furthermore, a significant portion of Mexico’s labor force works in the informal sector, limiting tax revenues and social protections. Mexico also relies heavily on fossil fuels and faces challenges in balancing economic growth with environmental sustainability. Mexico has a unique opportunity to capitalize on nearshoring due to U.S.-China tensions, but infrastructure and regulatory barriers remain. Democratic institutions face pressure from efforts to increase executive power, threats to autonomous institutions and electoral bodies, and political polarization.\nThe following recommendations address the country’s main challenges. On the security front, the government should strengthen civilian policing rather than rely primarily on the armed forces. This would require rooting out corruption in civilian law enforcement along with simultaneous efforts to improve the efficacy of the judicial system to reduce impunity. At the same time, the government should invest in modernizing and building the capacity of law enforcement officers. Enhancing cooperation with the United States to curb the flow of weapons into Mexico would also create obstacles for organized crime groups in the country.\nRegarding corruption, the government should strengthen anti-corruption agencies and improve transparency in public procurement and government contracts. The former would require the government to allow corruption investigations to run their course, unhindered, and to divulge information about the army upon request – which the government has tried to avoid until now. Independent oversight agencies also require adequate resources and independence to investigate and prosecute corruption effectively. By promoting judicial independence, the government would simultaneously strengthen checks and balances, thus preventing an excessive concentration of power. Promoting transparency, accountability and public participation will be vital to curbing the potential abuse of power.\nOn the economic front, the Sheinbaum administration should implement policies to encourage formal employment, such as tax incentives for small businesses transitioning to the formal economy. It should also expand social programs that target vulnerable groups and ensure that they promote upward mobility rather than dependence. To capitalize on nearshoring opportunities, the government should invest in logistics, ports and transportation infrastructure in order to promote domestic manufacturing and reduce the overall cost of The president has repeatedly expressed\n                    a deep distaste for all things legal. He has portrayed the law as an\n                    instrument of the ancien régime and legal requirements as hurdles in\n                    the way of attaining the “Fourth Transformation of Mexico.”58 A painful,\n                    paradigmatic illustration of this approach to the law is the executive\n                    decree that declared public works of infrastructure (such as the construc-\n                    tion of the Maya Train) to be “national security” issues, obliging all\n                    administrative units to issue the corresponding permits notwithstanding\n                    any statutory norm to the contrary.59\n                       An abundance of developments reveal tensions along the ﬁve dimen-\n                    sions that Shaffer and Sandholtz identify as deﬁning a goal-oriented\n                    understanding of the rule of law. To illustrate some of them, this chapter\n                    focuses on two clusters of developments. The ﬁrst is the frontal attack on\n                    the National Electoral Institute, the independent agency that remains the\n                    key guarantor of electoral regularity. The second is the militarization of\n                    state functions – ﬁrst, public security, and later a much wider set of state\n                    responsibilities, including the provisions of public services and the con-\n                    struction of public works.\n                       All of them reveal a willingness to eliminate checks and balances;\n                    a general disregard for the idea of reason-giving; a decline in the predict-\n                    ability of public action since many measures are processed speedily (with\n                    or without the intervention of a dominated legislature), often in open\n                    violation of legal requirements. As in other situations of autocratic\n                    legalism, the pattern is gradual, with the overall impact being greater\n                    than the sum of its parts. Intertwined with that pattern, however, is\n                    degree of legal contestation that has no precedent in Mexico. However, under the political system\n               progressively installed by the PRI, elections were rigged and won by the\n               person designated by the president. The PRI was to a certain extent\n               inclusive of various social groups and provided a system of elite\n               rotation.61 It also provided peace and stability in a country that had\n               endured signiﬁcant turmoil during the nineteenth century.62 But it was\n               not a democracy: there were formal elections, but no actual rule-of-law\n               preconditions to ensure free voting and political competition.\n                  When it ultimately became impossible to maintain the system without\n               changes, several constitutional reforms introduced electoral competition\n               and progressively built independent electoral authorities.63 An institu-\n               tion called IFE (Instituto Federal Electoral) was created in 1990, together\n               with parallel institutions at state level. In 1996, the IFE gained complete\n               independence from the executive, and in 2013 a constitutional reform\n               renamed the institution INE (Instituto Nacional Electoral) and gave it\n               more powers over the organization and monitoring of elections at state\n               level. The institution soon established itself as one marked by profession-\n               alization (its employees are career ofﬁcials) and a model of election\n               organization and supervision that included extensive input from the\n               citizenry and was grounded in administrative rule of law. Thus, the\n               voting booths in Mexico are managed by citizens who are selected on\n               the basis of their birth month, trained before the elections by the INE, and\n               60\n                  Tom Ginsburg deﬁnes the rule of law in the administration of elections as a key compo-\n                  nent of democracy. Further, for four years the presidency of the\n                    Court was held by Arturo Zaldívar, who was quickly criticized for\n                    cultivating an excessive closeness to the government. Under his presi-\n                    dency, the Court delayed decisions in many politically sensitive cases.\n                       In the electoral domain, however, the Court’s decision-making is\n                    subject to time limits. And its performance as regards Plan B has been\n                    admirably solid, even in the face of all imaginable kinds of pressure. It was in this subor-\n               dinated quality that the army was involved in the dark episodes of the\n               “dirty war” of the 1970s.83 Yet, during the gradual transition to democ-\n               racy of the 1980s and 1990s, the military was generally held in high regard\n               by the population – which would associate it with assistance during\n               natural disasters, among other tasks of that sort.\n                 The situation changed when Felipe Calderón won the presidency in\n               2006. Some two years later, although the matter had been mentioned\n               during his campaign, Calderón decided to launch a “war against drugs”\n               that put the army on the streets in several parts of the country without\n               any legal basis for doing so. While the government does not generally impose restrictions on anonymity or encryption for internet users, investigative reporting has revealed some ongoing restrictions on users of the Tor network, a censorship circumvention tool.\nAn investigation conducted between 2020 and October 2023 found that the Mexican government blocks 39 URLs from 21 Mexican government agencies for users of the Tor network.\n1\nA representative from the president’s office claimed that the “protection measures,” which have reportedly been in place for at least 12 years, are necessary to block traffic that is “malicious, automated, or that could be a threat.” In response, a Tor representative stated that the government’s actions are a disproportionate and an “isolating” way to safeguard against potential cyber harms.\n2\nData from the Open Observatory of Network Interference (OONI) showed that Tor remained widely accessible in Mexico during the coverage period, indicating that there had not been wider efforts to restrict Tor itself (see B1).\n3\nPreviously, in April 2022,\n4\nthe SCJN struck down the creation of a problematic biometric cell phone registry that had been established through a reform to the Federal Telecommunications and Broadcasting Law passed by Congress in April 2021. The court echoed criticism from digital rights organizations in its ruling, citing the registry’s unnecessary infringement on privacy rights and inadequate data safeguards.\n\n5\nUsers would have been required to join the registry when purchasing a SIM card or activating a new prepaid mobile line.\n6\n1\nJacbo Nájera and Miguel Trujillo, “Gobierno mexicano y la red Tor [Mexican government and the Tor network],” GitHub, October 2023,\nhttps://github.com/tor-gob/reporte-mexico\n.\n2\nJacobo Nájera and Miguel Trujillo, “Mexican government faces criticism for blocking portions of the safe internet,” Global Voices, October 12, 2023,\nhttps://advox.globalvoices.org/2023/10/12/mexican-government-faces-crit…\n.\n3\nOONI, “OONI Measurement Aggregation Toolkit (MAT): Tor Test, Mexico,” OONI Explorer, accessed September 2024,\nhttps://explorer.ooni.org/chart/mat?probe_cc=MX&since=2023-09-16&until=…\n.\n4\nDarinka Rodríguez, “La Suprema Corte de México invalida la creación de un padrón de datos biométricos para usuarios de celulares” [Mexican Supreme Court invalidates the creation of a biometric registry for mobile phone users], El País, April 25, 2022,\nhttps://elpais.com/mexico/2022-04-25/la-suprema-corte-de-mexico-invalid…\n.\n5\n“Mexico’s president can prevent a privacy disaster: veto the new biometric mobile phone registry,” AccessNow, April 16, 2021,\nhttps://www.accessnow.org/mexicos-new-biometric-mobile-phone-registry/\n; High-profile abuses of digital spying technologies meant for law enforcement purposes continued to emerge during the coverage period, but they have not been thoroughly investigated by authorities.\nIn February 2024, an investigation from R3D detailed the functions of the Cyberspace Operations Center (COC), a covert division of SEDENA created in 2016 to conduct “military operations in cyberspace.”\n1\nAccording to the investigation, the COC conducts social media monitoring of users who criticize the Mexican military or the federal government, at times creating inauthentic user accounts in an attempt to infiltrate trusted networks online and uncover more information about critical users. The investigation found that the COC uses a specialized software created by Israeli company WebintPro, called HIWIRE, to monitor social media activities and identify links between users, as well as to deploy bots to “exert soft influence on public opinion” (see B5).\n2\nThese activities are known through leaked documents;\n3\nthere is no legal basis for the operations of the COC in existing Mexican law and the contract that SEDENA signed to acquire HIWIRE has not been made publicly available.\n\nThe Mexican military is reported to be one of the world’s largest users of Pegasus spyware, which can surveil all activities on mobile devices with no apparent signs of a breach.\n4\nPegasus has been used to target those investigating government corruption and human rights abuses in Mexico.\n5\nA joint investigation by Citizen Lab and the Mexican civil society organization R3D revealed that two human rights defenders, Jorge Santiago Aguirre Espinosa and María Luisa Aguilar Rodríguez, both working at the Miguel Agustín Pro Juárez Human Rights Center (Centro PRODH), were targeted by Pegasus between June and September 2022. According to Citizen Lab, the alleged timing of the surveillance suggests that the military was involved in these cases, though it was not able to confirm this. At the time the spyware was apparently active on Aguirre and Aguilar’s devices, Centro PRODH had been investigating past human rights abuses committed by the Mexican Army and providing support for the relatives of those who were forcibly disappeared by the military.\n6\nIn October 2022, the #EjércitoEspía investigation, coordinated by several civil society organizations and media outlets, documented three additional cases of suspected military espionage using Pegasus. Human rights defender Raymundo Ramos and two journalists, Ricardo Raphael and one from the outlet Animal Político, were reportedly surveilled with Pegasus between 2019 and 2021.\n7\nThe evidence presented in the investigation, which includes forensic analysis by Citizen Lab, confirmed that the victims were targeted with zero-click exploits, which do not require any action from victims and are virtually undetectable.\n8\nAll three individuals had recently denounced human rights abuses by the Mexican armed forces, suggesting that the Mexican military was responsible for the illegal spying.\n9\nIn March 2023, the same organizations that produced the #EjércitoEspía investigation released new evidence about the surveillance of human rights defender Raymundo Ramos.\n10\nInternal documents obtained from SEDENA appeared to conclusively demonstrate that the military used Pegasus to spy on Ramos through the highly secretive Military Intelligence Center (CMI), which lacks any legal basis for spying on civilians. According to the investigation, the CMI operates under the command of military leadership and spied on Ramos in order to disrupt his journalistic investigation into the army’s human rights abuses.\n11\nIn May 2023, the\nNew York Times\nreported that Alejandro Encinas, the country’s undersecretary for human rights and a close ally of President López Obrador, had been targeted with Pegasus spyware. Encinas had recently investigated potential abuses by the military and had been publicly critical of the armed forces.\n12\nIn June, during the coverage period, the\nWashington Post\npublished an investigation reporting that historian Camilo Vicente Ovalle, who coordinates a truth commission about Mexico’s “Dirty War” as part of Encinas’ office, was also targeted with Pegasus in the latter half of 2022;\n13\na development which was condemned by the truth commission’s Historical Clarification Mechanism and by digital rights organizations.\n\n14\nPresident López Obrador denied the evidence presented by the organizations and the media outlets, repeatedly claiming that his government had not used Pegasus to spy on Encinas or other figures.\n15\nAfter the October 2022 #EjércitoEspía investigation was published, López Obrador dismissed claims that the government had spied on journalist Ricardo Raphael because “it would be a waste of time” to do so. He also claimed that the army does not spy, but rather does “intelligence.”\n16\nDespite these revelations, authorities have been slow to investigate, and past cases have continued to go unpunished.\n17\nIn January 2023, the INAI ordered SEDENA to carry out a thorough search and provide information related to the contracts that the military signed with the company Comercializadora Antsua, the exclusive supplier of the Pegasus spyware in Mexico.\n18\nAfter SEDENA refused to comply for more than a year, in June 2024, after the coverage period, a court ordered the military to turn over the documents.\n19\nThe government was first implicated in the use of Pegasus when the results of the Pegasus Project investigation were published in July 2021. Leaked data from NSO Group, originally accessed by Forbidden Stories and Amnesty International and shared with 15 media organizations, confirmed and expanded upon prior reporting on the Mexican government’s use of Pegasus against critical voices.\n20\nSome 15,000 phone numbers from a leaked list of 50,000—which are presumed to belong to the targets of NSO clients—belonged to people located in Mexico, including journalists and politicians; the Mexican bloc was the largest in the entire list.\n21\nIn November 2021, the Attorney General’s Office (FGR) announced its first detention in the Pegasus investigation: Juan Carlos García Rivera, an employee in one of the dozen private companies that served as intermediaries between the Mexican government and NSO Group. García Rivera was accused of spying on journalist Carmen Aristegui via Pegasus in a way that “affected, limited, and undermined her freedom of expression.”\n22\nIn January 2024, a judge in Mexico City acquitted García Rivera, determining that Aristegui had been spied on with Pegasus for her journalistic work but that prosecutors had failed to prove that García Rivera was directly responsible.\n23\nIn response, Article 19, R3D, and SocialTIC emphasized that actions seeking to ensure accountability must continue.\n24\nOfficials have access to other surveillance tools with interception capabilities. In April 2023, Citizen Lab reported that Israeli spyware vendor QuaDream had been contracted by several government clients, including Mexico, to provide surveillance technology.\n25\nLike Pegasus, QuaDream is reportedly a zero-click exploit. ENVIRONMENTAL, FORESTS, AND OTHER NATURAL RESOURCE ASPECTS\n76. Policy measures supported by the DPL are expected to have significant positive effects on\nclimate change and the environment. The WBG’s environmental analysis of the DPL finds that most\npolicies supported, mainly under pillar 2, would have significant positive effects on Mexico’s climate\nchange mitigation and environmental priorities. Policy measures of pillar 2 will enhance the\nenvironmental and climate change resilience under existing laws and programs that promote\nenvironmental sustainability and disaster risk management. Mexico’s institutional and regulatory\nframework to avoid, reduce, mitigate, and manage adverse environmental effects is sufficiently robust\nand can address potential negative environmental effects arising from these policy reforms.\n77. The policy measures will support Mexico in complying with its NDC by fostering low carbon and\nclimate-resilient growth, enhancing NPA management and forest conservation, and establishing\neffective disaster risk management. These policy measures will specifically strengthen the country’s\nadaptation capacity, particularly in the most vulnerable municipalities, and enhance resilience of urban\nand rural landscapes. The DPL will foster mandatory mitigation measures for land use changes in forest\nlands (PA 5), enforce measures to avoid deforestation (PA 6), and enhance Mexico’s area under\nconservation status (PA 8), contributing to the preservation of carbon sinks that are essential for Mexico\nto meet its NDC. The DPL will also strengthen disaster risk management (PA 4) which is expected to have\npositive environmental effects by fostering enhanced resilience and disaster responsiveness nationally.\nPolicy reforms under pillar 1 around digital financial inclusion could have longer-term positive\nenvironmental effects.\n78. Mexico has a solid and comprehensive national environmental legislation to promote\nsustainability and resilience measures supported by this operation. The legislation was formally\ndeveloped based on the General Law of Ecological Equilibrium and Environmental Protection (LGEEPA) of\n1988. Since then, Mexico has established laws, policies, programs, and provided resources that set\nenvironmental requirements to investments in terms of managing environmental impacts and waste,\ncontrolling pollution, and addressing material efficiency and climate change, among other. Regarding the\nlatter, the General Climate Change Law of 2012 supports the transition to a competitive, sustainable, and\nlow-carbon economy; reduces the vulnerability of the population and ecosystems; and assigns\nresponsibilities within the Government. The GoM has committed to supporting climate change mitigation\nand adaptation as reflected in its updated NDC under the United Nations Framework Convention on\nClimate Change.\n79. On November 22, 2021, the GoM issued a Presidential Accord declaring the execution of certain\ninfrastructure projects a matter of national security and public interest and ordered federal agencies to\nPage 41\n\nThe World Bank\nMexico Inclusive and Sustainable Economic Growth DPL (P178224)\nissue provisional environmental and social permits within five business days from the time of the\nrequest, to expedite the execution of said projects. On December 14, 2021, the Mexican Supreme Court\npartially suspended the Presidential Accord in response to the constitutional controversy raised by the\nNational Institute of Transparency, Access to Information, and Protection of Personal Data (INAI) with\nrespect to any effects and consequences of the Presidential Accord that may derive from the classification\nof information as of public interest and/or national security. These legal challenges may take up to a year\nto be resolved, and project-specific provisional permits issued could be challenged by affected parties in\ncourts, seeking temporary suspension of the provisions of the Accord, or an injunction on project-specific\nrelated activities, until courts make a final decision. SEMARNAT has informed that, so far, the Accord has\nnot been implemented since approval and that it continues to apply Mexico’s environmental management\nframework, confirming that all environmental legislation remains valid and in place, and would be\nenforced during the operation’s timeline. However, the potential implementation of the Accord poses a\nsignificant risk that could weaken Mexico’s environmental management framework and undermine the\npolicy measures supported by the DPL under Pillar 2 (see paragraph 95).\n5.3. PFM, DISBURSEMENT AND AUDITING ASPECTS\n80. Mexico’s Public Financial Management (PFM) framework is mostly aligned with good\ninternational practices, including the use of budget resources and the FOREX internal control system\nmanaged by the Mexican Central Bank. According to the latest Fiscal Transparency Evaluation (FTE) of\nthe IMF (dated October 2018), Mexico scores relatively well compared to other Latin American countries\nand emerging market economies that have undergone such evaluations. Out of the 48 principles across\nfour pillars in the FTE, Mexico meets 16 principles at the basic level, 9 principles at the good level, and 15\nprinciples at the advanced level. The areas of strength include fiscal reporting, forecasting, and budgeting\nand resource revenue management. Conversely, the areas for improvement include the need to\nstrengthen the medium-term fiscal framework, the medium-term budget framework, and fiscal risk\nanalysis and management.\n81. Government commitment to support PFM reforms. Mexico’s budget legal and control\nframework is comprehensive, and the country has demonstrated a good track record in implementing\nPFM reforms. One of the recent major reforms focused on public sector accountability, integrity, and\ntransparency with the establishment of the Law63 of the National Anti-Corruption System, which aims to\nimprove coordination among different oversight entities and civil society organizations.64 However,\ncorruption control is an ongoing concern in the public sector.65 In addition, Mexico adopted accrual\naccounting, harmonizing accounting standards across all levels of government through the creation of the\nNational Council of Accounting Harmonization (Consejo Nacional de Armonización Contable) and the\nenactment of the General Government Accounting Law in 2008.\n63 The Law of the National Anti-Corruption System was issued in 2016 and reformed in 2021.\n64 The members of the National Anti-Corruption System include representatives from civil society, the heads of the Supreme\nAudit Institution, the Ministry of Public Administration, the anti-corruption agency, and INAI, among others.\n65 Mexico scored 31 out of 100 in the Corruption Perception Index prepared by Transparency International, below most of its\nregional peers.\nPage 42", "excerpt_sha256": Leveraging the Anti-Money Laundering Efforts to\n                   Support Anti-Corruption Efforts1\n\nA. Interaction between Mexico’s AML and AC Frameworks\n\n1.      Corruption and money laundering (ML) are symbiotic as they tend to co-occur. The\npresence of one tends to create and reciprocally reinforce the incidence of the other. 2 The strongest\nlink between the two crimes is the need for corruption proceeds to be laundered by the criminals,\nwhich implicates the AML framework. Some of the AML measures—such as the enhanced due\ndiligence measures applicable to Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs) that pose high risk for corruption\nand the filing of Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) by reportable entities—could, in turn, be\nhelpful in detecting and preventing corruption in the first place. Furthermore, corruption could\nundermine the proper functioning and effectiveness of the AML/CFT framework (e.g., independence\nand governance of AML/CFT institutions). It is therefore important that frameworks aimed at\ntackling corruption and money laundering work in tandem to tackle financial crimes and limit their\nimpact on the macroeconomy to help ensure a sustainable and inclusive economic growth and\npromote a conducive investment environment.\n\n2.      The 2020 National Risk Assessment on ML and terrorism financing ranked laundering\nof corruption proceeds among the highest risks in Mexico. The preliminary results from the most\nrecent update to the National Risk Assessment confirm that corruption remains among the highest\nML threats. Therefore, it is particularly relevant in the context of Mexico to further refine the\nunderstanding of risks of laundering of domestic corruption to highlight the key sectors at risk and\nthe macroeconomic impact of those crimes. Such understanding of risks of corruption and\nlaundering of its proceeds could help better inform policy determination under the AML and AC\nframeworks and ensure their better integration and complementarity.\n\n3.      The recognition of corruption as a substantial problem in Mexico led to the 2015\nreforms. The National Anti-Corruption System (Sistema Nacional Anticorrupción or SNA) was\nintroduced following amendments to the constitution, along with a package of new laws and legal\namendments that provide for the regulatory and institutional framework in the fight against\ncorruption. 3 The SNA is coordinated by the SNA Coordination Committee comprising seven\n\n1 Prepared by Adrian Wardzynski, with research support from Alessandro D’Amelio (both LEG).\n\n2 Countries that struggle to tackle take decisive actions against corruption usually have lower levels of compliance\n\nwith AML standards. See C. Verdugo, Compliance with the AML/CFT International Standard: Lessons from a Cross-\nCountry Analysis, IMF Working Paper, WP/11/177.\n3 In addition to changes to Article 113 of the Constitution, the AC legal package included the General Law on the\n\nNational Anti-Corruption System (Ley General del Sistema Nacional Anticorrupción), the General Law on\nAdministrative Responsibilities (Ley General de Responsabilidades Administrativas), the Law of Control and\nAccountability of the Federation (Ley de Fiscalización y Rendición de Cuentas de la Federación), amendments to the\nOrganic Law of the Federal Court of Administrative Justice (Ley Orgánica del Tribunal Federal de Justicia\nAdministrativa), amendments to the Organic Law of the Attorney’s General Office (Ley Orgánica de la Fiscalía General\nde la República), amendments to the Federal Penal Code (Código Penal Federal), amendments to the Organic Law of\nFederal Public Administration (Ley Orgánica de la Administración Pública Federal).\n\n\n84   INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND\n\nMEXICO\n\n\n\nnational institutions. The Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) and the AML supervisors, i.e., the National\nBanking and Securities Commission (Comisión Nacional Bancaria y de Valores or CNBV) and the tax\nauthority (Servicio de Administración Tributaria or SAT), are indirectly represented at the Committee\nthrough the Ministry of Public Administration (MPA).\n\n4.      Policies of the SNA could reflect better the high risk of laundering of proceeds of\ncorruption. The SNA Coordination Committee approved the National Anti-Corruption Policy\n(Prioridades e implementación de la Política Nacional or PNA) in January 2020 and the National\nImplementation Plan in January 2022. The overall effectiveness of the PNA will also depend on the\nstrength of Mexico’s AML framework, especially given that corruption is among the highest ML\nthreats in Mexico. As part of operationalization of these policies, the priorities for the PNA and its\nimplementation plan benchmarks should reflect AML measures and close coordination with AML\nauthorities.\n\n5.      Coordinating policy priorities for AML and AC could achieve better outcomes. Such\ncoordination could ensure common understanding of risks of corruption and ML and the\nvulnerabilities of different sectors for misuse, better allocation of resources, and prioritization of\nboth frameworks to achieve common outcomes. At the operational level, the MPA, FIU, and AML\nsupervisors should exchange information and cooperate by drawing on the synergies between their\nmandates and relevant information which would enable taking joint action against corruption and\nits proceeds. Given the importance of financial intelligence produced by the FIU to detect and\ndisrupt proceeds of corruption, as well as the role of banks and other financial and non-financial\ngatekeepers in preventing access of “dirty money” into the formal and informal economy, it is\nimportant that the AML and AC policies are coordinated to ensure that the mutually reinforcing\neffects of the AML and AC frameworks are fully utilized.\n\nB. Laundering of Proceeds of Corruption and AML Preventative Measures\n\n6.      PEPs are subject to enhanced due diligence under the AML framework in Mexico. The\nAML financial sector supervisor in Mexico, the CNBV, has dedicated criteria that it uses to verify\nwhether banks and other financial institutions under its supervisory purview are compliant with the\napplicable preventive measures for PEPs. The CNBV has also published guidance to financial entities\non the risks of corruption and related money laundering, which includes details on the necessary\ncontrols related to PEPs. There is also a list of PEPs published by the Ministry of Finance and Public\nCredit to further aid compliance by regulated entities.\n\n7.       The implementation of AML controls applicable to PEPs could be further strengthened\nand the major gaps in the legal framework of the non-financial sector addressed. The CNBV\nfound numerous non-compliance issues in enhanced due diligence processes applied by financial\ninstitutions in relation to PEPs. These include inadequate risk assessment and monitoring of\ntransactions to ensure alignment with the roles, level, and responsibilities of PEPs, failures to\ndetermine PEPs that may be controlling legal entities, reliance on outdated lists of PEPs, as well as\nother documentation and quality of information issues. While these are primarily about aspects of\n\n\n\n                                                                   INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND       85\n\nMEXICO\n\n\n\neffective implementation, the regulatory framework in the non-financial sector is not yet fully in\nplace. Currently, the Designated Non-Financial Businesses and Professions (DNFBPs)—such as\nlawyers, notaries, accountants, real estate agents, or Trust and Company Service Providers—are not\nlegally obliged under Mexico’s AML legal framework to carry out due diligence checks in relation to\nPEPs. 4 This is particularly important given the key role that such gatekeepers play in laundering\nproceeds of corruption through activities such as running and managing of business activities of\nlegal entities or purchasing of expensive real estate, among the most common techniques to\nlaunder corruption proceeds in Mexico.\n\n8.      STRs filed by the AML regulated entities are an important aspect of detecting financial\ncrimes, including corruption. The FIU indicated that it receives more than 340,000 STRs per year.\nThese cover suspicions of money laundering and its underlying financial crimes such as corruption\nor tax crimes.\n\n9.       Mexico's legal framework for STRs needs significant improvements, especially in\nrelation to DNFBPs. Most of the technical deficiencies in relation to the STRs identified in the\nFinancial Action Task Force (FATF) Mutual Evaluation Report published in 2018 remain unresolved. 5\nIn the case of the STRs obligations applicable to financial institutions, there are issues with the\napplicable timeframes and the level of suspicion required to trigger filing. In the case of the DNFBPs,\nthe existing obligation to file Notices should be amended to ensure comprehensive coverage and\nalignment with the FATF Recommendations. This translates directly into the low levels of reports\nfiled by the DNFBPs and the inability to effectively sanction such practices. More broadly, the overall\nAML regulatory and supervisory framework over the DNFBPs requires substantial strengthening. 6\n\n10.      Mexico should address deficiencies in the implementation of the STR obligations and\nboost the capacity of the FIU to prioritize the STRs related to PEPs. In addition to addressing\nthe legal deficiencies, the implementation of STR obligations should be further strengthened. Based\non the supervisory activities of the CNBV, there are recurrent issues in the accuracy of the customer\ndata that can compromise the integrity and reliability of the client records and related filing\nobligations. Further deficiencies were found by the CNBV in the application of the minimum criteria\nfor the filing of reports under the “24-hours process” and the quality of information included in the\nSTRs (i.e., the description of the underlying operations and the reasons for the suspicions). The FIU\nshould further promote compliance with best practices on the filing of STRs, including those related\nto PEPs and suspicious activities related to laundering generated by corruption, and prioritize\nensuing compliance and raising awareness of the DNBFPs. Given the large number of reports\nreceived by the FIU, the authorities should also ensure that it has adequate resources, both human\nand technological, to carry out sufficient screening of the received reports while prioritizing the STRs\nrelated to PEPs.\n\n4 See the Financial Action Task Force Follow-up Report on Mexico published in May 2023 and available at\n\nhttps://www.fatf-gafi.org/content/dam/fatf-gafi/fur/Follow-Up-Report-Mexico-2023.pdf.coredownload.pdf.\n5 For the 2018 Mutual Evaluation Report, see https://www.fatf-gafi.org/en/publications/Mutualevaluations/Mer-\n\nmexico-2018.html.\n6 See the 2023 Follow-Up Report available at https://www.fatf-gafi.org/content/dam/fatf-gafi/fur/Follow-Up-Report-\n\nMexico-2023.pdf.coredownload.pdf.\n\n\n86   INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND\n\nMEXICO\n\n\n\n11.      Misuse of legal entities is among the techniques most used in Mexico to launder\nproceeds of crimes, including corruption. Shell companies and front companies are commonly\nutilized to conceal the beneficial ownership of assets and funds as well as the true purpose of\ntransactions. These are also used by PEPs in Mexico to cover payment of bribes and embezzle public\nfunds.\n\n12.      Implementation of the AML framework in Mexico does not adequately ensure\navailability of beneficial ownership information. The AML framework requires that regulated\nentities identify beneficial ownership information as part of their customer due diligence processes.\nThere can be however doubts about the veracity of this source of beneficial ownership information\nin light of the effectiveness issues. 7 As identified by the CNBV, there are significant issues in the\nprocedures followed by financial institutions to identify beneficial owners including for PEPs.\nDeficiencies have been identified in the collection and review of the necessary data and\ndocumentation that is essential for this largely factual test. The difficulties in reliance on the\nbeneficial ownership information obtained through regulated entities were also acknowledged by\nthe FIU that requires it for the purposes of financial analysis and production of financial intelligence\nreports for law enforcement agencies. The prosecutors generally rely on their own analysis—\nincluding review of the legal structure, board minutes, and field-based investigations—for the\ndetermination of beneficial ownership information. Given the key value of beneficial ownership\ninformation in tackling financial crimes, the authorities should step up supervisory oversight and\napply proportional and dissuasive sanctions in cases of non-compliance. There are also significant\nissues in the legal framework applicable to the DNFBPs, including in relation to the understanding of\nthe legal and control structure of the customers, which should be addressed through legislative\nchanges.\n\n13.     The new beneficial ownership information requirements arising under the tax laws are\ncurrently underutilized for AML purposes. The amendments to the Federal Tax Code in\nNovember 2021, which took effect in January 2022, introduced new obligations pursuant to Article\n32-B Ter on legal entities and their service providers to obtain and report beneficial ownership\ninformation to the Mexican tax authorities (SAT). These new rules were introduced to enable the SAT\nto obtain such information upon request and then report to foreign tax authorities in compliance\nwith requirements arising under the international tax transparency standards overseen by the Global\nForum on Transparency and Exchange of Information. 8 While these may also be of value for the\nbroader entity transparency objectives and tackling of financial crimes, they have not been used to\ndate in this context. Moreover, given the specific rationale for the introduction of these new\nobligations, there is no specific database that can be consulted by other competent authorities and\nregulated entities at the SAT for the beneficial ownership information that it has the ability to\nrequest. The SAT also does not verify the information. Mexico should introduce a beneficial\n\n7 For an analysis regarding the overall low effectiveness of the AML preventive measures, including those relating to\n\nbeneficial ownership requirements, see the 2018 Mutual Evaluation Report of Mexico adopted by the FATF and\navailable at https://www.fatf-gafi.org/en/countries/detail/Mexico.html.\n8 See https://www.oecd.org/publications/global-forum-on-transparency-and-exchange-of-information-for-tax-\n\npurposes-mexico-2023-second-round-6fd9ab78-en.htm.\n\n\n\n                                                                            INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND            87\n\nMEXICO\n\n\n\nownership registry and establish relevant processes to ensure that the information collected is\naccurate, adequate, and up to date. Beneficial ownership information should also be required to be\ncollected and verified as part of the public procurement process.\n\nC. Prosecution of Money Laundering and Corruption\n\n14.      The jurisdiction and cooperation between the specialized prosecutor offices\nresponsible for money laundering and corruption in Mexico should be enhanced. Money\nlaundering cases are prosecuted by the Specialized Prosecutor Office for Organized Crime (Fiscalía\nEspecializada en Materia de Delincuencia Organizada or FEMDO). This office can also carry out\nparallel investigations of money laundering and other financial crimes, such as corruption, if they are\nconsidered of high impact. In 2019 the Specialized Prosecutor Office for Corruption (Fiscalía\nEspecializada en Combate a la Corrupción or FMCCO) was established. While this office was\nexpected to take the lead on corruption-related cases, it has mainly dealt with matters relating to\nabuse of office, which is one of the forms of corruption. Corruption and bribery cases are not among\nits top five categories of cases and it has not yet prosecuted any high-level corruption cases. The\nauthorities should clarify the jurisdiction between the FEMDO and FEMCCO and also provide for\ntheir close cooperation to avoid fragmentation that would adversely affect the effectiveness to\nprosecute corruption cases and related money laundering.\n\n15.     The authorities should ensure that there are strict AC policies applicable to the law\nenforcement authorities, at both federal and state levels, as well as the judiciary. The level of\ncorruption in Mexico can affect the functioning of the law enforcement system and undermines the\ncapacity to investigate and prosecute corruption and money laundering. The number prosecutions\nand convictions relating to corruption and money laundering is not commensurate with Mexico’s\nrisk profile. The authorities should take steps to increase resources, capacity, and expertise as well as\nensure adequate budget of the law enforcement authorities. Confiscation and asset recovery should\nbe seen as major policy objectives within the national AML and AC policies and implementation\nplans in order to ensure that crime does not pay.\n\n\n\n\n88   INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND", "excerpt_sha256": "cbaeabc12eb75d780c6f0f351a804d89cb38d728fd290435b2a3739b815d8dca", "verification_status": "accepted", "verification_notes": []}, {"evidence_id": "BATCH-0016-E022", "source_id": "SRC-684988a395d1a128", "url": "https://www.banxico.org.mx/publications-and-press/imf-article-iv-consultation-for-mexico/%7B2B9230B7-CC63-5B20-E173-F5E94D116BC9%7D.pdf", "title": "IMF Country Report No. 23/356 — Mexico", "publisher": "Banco de México / International Monetary Fund", "raw_sha256": "f93592f437a264c95c4c753720221642f0dd636d55e012cef97b95d1b59a294a", "fact_summary": "The IMF found limited foreign-bribery risk but reported no completed foreign-bribery prosecution, inadequate whistleblower protection, unclear corporate liability, and unresolved deficiencies in PEP monitoring, beneficial-ownership identification, suspicious-transaction reporting, and DNFBP supervision.
