JULY 2023\n Submission to the 45th session of the UPR Working Group, January-February                         LANGUAGE: ENGLISH\n 2024                                                                        2\n                                                                                                   amnesty.org\n\n19. Amnesty´s report The Age of Women: Stigma and violence against women protesters 36 documented human rights\n         violations committed bylaw enforcement officials against women demanding a life free from violence in Sinaloa, the\n         State of Mexico, Mexico City, Guanajuato, and Quintana Roo in 2020. These violations include excessive and\n         unnecessary use of force, illegal and arbitrary arrests, gender-based verbal and physical abuse, and sexual\n         violence, stigmatization of feminist demonstrations as “violent” as well as discriminatory bias against women\n         covering their faces. Currently, no one has been held to account for these abuses.\n\n     20. The criminal justice system is often used as a deterrence mechanism for those protesting especially for land,\n         territorial, environmental and climate rights. Since the last review, Amnesty has documented cases of the\n         criminalization of protest.37 These cases show a tendency to criminalize leaders and human rights defenders by\n         using vague or broad criminal offences or fabricating criminal charges against them. Violations of rights in these\n         cases include lack of due process and access to justice, prolonged trial processes with the constant threat of\n         deprivation of liberty, as well as lack of prior informed consent in the cases of indigenous communities, and\n         impunity.\n\n\nSAFETY OF JOURNALISTS\n\n     21. Mexico is one of the most dangerous countries in the world for journalists. 2020 38 and 202239 were some of the\n         deadliest years in Mexican history for the press, with at least 19 and 13 journalists killed respectively because of\n         their work, more than in 202140 and 2019.41\n\n     22. At the federal level, since 2012, Mexico has had a Mechanism for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders and\n         Journalists (“the Mechanism”),42 which provides certain protection measures for people who have received attacks\n         or threats. Currently, the Mechanism benefits more than 500 journalists,43 but from 2017 to 2021, at least seven\n         journalists have been killed despite having been afforded protection by the Mechanism. 44\n\n     23. Furthermore, many cases remain without adequate investigation and the Mechanism continued to fall short of its\n         goal to safeguard the lives and safety of these groups.45 The Mechanism has not yet provided a strategy to respond\n         to digital attacks and unlawful surveillance, such as from the NSO Group’s spyware Pegasus. 46\n\nMILITARIZATION\n\n     24. Mexico has relied on a heavily militarized public security strategy. A constitutional amendment in 2019 47 created\n         the National Guard (GN), which was intended to be under civilian control. However, the GN is heavily influenced\n         by the Armed Forces (AF); a former army general is in command, and most of its members were formerly part of\n         the AF. The fifth transitory article in the constitutional reforms provided that the AF would participate in public\n         security tasks for up to five years while the GN becomes fully operational.48\n\n     25. In 2020, an executive decree formally involved the AF in public security tasks until 2024, 49 a period that was\n         recently extended after the Congress agreed to keep the army on the streets until 2028, 50 without a strategy for\n         demilitarization of public security and law enforcement agencies and police reform. In November 2022, the\n         Supreme Court resolved that the Presidential Decree of 2020 allowing the permanent participation of AF in public\n         security operations until 2024 was constitutional. 51\n\n     26. In September 2022, Congress approved an initiative that places the GN formally under the control of Mexico´s\n         Ministry of National Defence (SEDENA). 52 However, on 18 April 2023, the Supreme Court struck down the transfer\n         of the GN to SEDENA.53\n\n     27. The GN is among the ten federal institutions with the highest number of complaints for human rights violations.\n         The NHRC has received 1,200 complaints against the GN, since its creation in 2019 up to September 2022. 54\n         These complaints related to arbitrary detentions, torture and other ill-treatment, enforced disappearances and other\n         violations. As for SEDENA and SEMAR (Secretariat of the Navy), from 2019 to September 2022, the NHRC collected\n         1,604 complaints and 1,553 respectively, regarding multiple violations of human rights, including torture and other\n         ill-treatment, unlawful killings, enforced disappearances and arbitrary detentions. 55\n\n\n\n                                                                                                 INDEX AMR 41/6992/2023\n MEXICO: RUSHING HEADFIRST INTO AN ABYSS OF HUMAN RIGHTS?                                        JULY 2023\n Submission to the 45th session of the UPR Working Group, January-February                       LANGUAGE: ENGLISH\n 2024                                                                        3\n                                                                                                 amnesty.org\n\n28. Participation of the AF in the public life of Mexico has increased the probability of being a victim of sexual torture\n         when detained; led to more violations of judicial guarantees during detention; and fostered a lack of truth,\n         transparency and accountability in its operations.56\n\n     29. In addition, military personnel have been directly linked to the enforced disappearance of the 43 Ayotzinapa\n         students, extrajudicial executions and cases of torture and other ill-treatment.57\n\n\n\nRECOMMENDATIONS FOR ACTION BY THE STATE UNDER REVIEW\nAmnesty International calls on the government of Mexico to:\n\nNational human rights framework\n     30. As Mexico previously agreed to do, strengthen the National Human Rights Commission so that it complies with the\n         Paris Principles and ensure that its recommendations are in line with international human rights norms and\n         standards, including consideration of the needs of victims as well as of standards on comprehensive reparations.\n\n     31. Ensure that law enforcement personnel and those working in the criminal justice system are provided with adequate\n         resources to carry out their functions efficiently and in accordance with international human rights standards,\n         including decent and appropriate compensation and working conditions.\n\nViolence against women and girls\n     32. Publicly acknowledge the scale of the problem of feminicides and disappearances in Mexico, as well as the failings\n         in the investigations into these crimes, and send a clear message that these crimes will no longer be tolerated or\n         go unpunished.\n\n     33. Guarantee full reparations family members of feminicide victims in line with the “Basic Principles and Guidelines\n         on the Right to a Remedy and Reparation for Victims of Gross Violations of International Human Rights Law and\n         Serious Violations of International Humanitarian Law” and the CEDAW General Recommendation 35.\n\n     34. Investigate the problem of failures in criminal investigations of crimes of violence against women, especially\n         feminicides and disappearances and issue recommendations that address the aspects highlighted in this report,\n         such as excessive workloads, failure to investigate, the application of a gender perspective, the collection and\n         safeguarding of evidence and the need for training of public servants in Public Prosecutors’ Offices.\n\n\nSocial Protest\n   35. Publicly recognize the legitimacy of the right to peaceful protest, facilitate and protect persons exercising this right,\n        and abstain from their stigmatization and criminalization.\n\n     36. Carry out prompt, thorough, independent and impartial investigations, with a gender and intersectional perspective,\n         into violations of human rights occurring before, during and after protests.\n\n     37. Guarantee access to justice and full reparation for victims of human rights violations in the context of protests in\n         line with the “Basic Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Remedy and Reparation for Victims of Gross\n         Violations of International Human Rights Law and Serious Violations of International Humanitarian Law”.\n\n     38. Amend the National Law on the Use of Force (specifically Articles 27, 28 and 36) in line with international human\n         rights law, the “Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials”, the UN Code of\n         Conduct for Law Enforcement Officials, and in accordance with relevant judgments issued by the IACHR.\n\n\n\n\n                                                                                                   INDEX AMR 41/6992/2023\n MEXICO: RUSHING HEADFIRST INTO AN ABYSS OF HUMAN RIGHTS?
